doc.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Los Angeles after the war and Westlake
title: Westlake teachers and lessons with Lloyd Reese
summary: Kenny Farrar and David Baskerville teach arranging; he studies saxophone with Lloyd Reese, who has him run chord arpeggios.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Who were your instructors? Who was on the faculty there?

Nobody famous. We had Kenny Farrar. He was one of the arranging teachers. And David Baskerville, who later became head of the program at Denver University, I think, or Colorado University at Denver maybe. Kenny Farrar is still around. He was a drummer, and he wrote arrangements, the first drummer I knew that did that. Anyway, just showing me the basics, and right away I started writing charts. Everybody thought I was some kind of whiz, because I could put down a lot of the stuff that I had heard. And I started studying privately, saxophone, with Lloyd Reese, who was a trumpet player and a teacher. He taught a lot of people. Dexter Gordon and Eric Dolphy are the famous ones. Lloyd, he didn‟t get as deep with me as he probably did with some of the other guys. He had – his impression of me was not great, because he told me one day that I reminded him of another student at Westlake College who was a little more advanced than me. I didn‟t really dig this guy. I figured that if Lloyd had that impression of me, he was not wild about me. But he had me running chords, arpeggio style, all the chords

through every – to a tune, every bar, going through the whole 32 bars to a tune playing arpeggios of the harmony. I got that – was able to do that, although I could have used a little more philosophy, I think. But that was not forthcoming. So I made due with what I got. It turned out to be a good thing, because a few months later I auditioned for a band here that had made some records which I had heard on the radio. His name was Ike Carpenter. On the records, he‟d use Lucky Thompson, who had a chordal approach which really knocked me out, because I was – I loved his sound. And I was able to do that from this thing that I had been studying with Lloyd. So that came in handy. But as time went by, I learned that that was not playing jazz. That was running chords.
